Advanced Security being disabled would affect related security features generally, but the specific gating mechanism described here is the enterprise-level policy toggle, not GHAS enablement alone. Public-vs-private repository status isn't the actual restriction on this specific feature. And branch protection on a default branch governs how changes merge into that branch — it has no bearing on whether a security scanning feature can be enabled at all.

question: Using Copilot Chat for Business, you make requests but get no suggestions back at all. What's the most likely explanation?
options: A) You've exhausted your premium request quota, blocking all suggestions
B) You've disabled suggestions matching public code, and the filter is suppressing every viable completion because they'd all match public patterns
C) The new repository is private, so Copilot Chat can't access the code
D) The active file is blank, so Copilot Chat has no context to work with
explanation: When the public-code-matching filter is set to block, any candidate suggestion resembling public code gets suppressed before it's ever shown — if every plausible completion for a given prompt happens to closely match existing public code, you can end up seeing nothing at all, which is a real, specific cause of a completely empty response. Running out of premium request quota would typically produce an explicit quota/limit message rather than silent empty output. Private repository status doesn't block Copilot Chat's core functioning — Business/Enterprise Copilot is specifically built to work with private, proprietary code, not restricted away from it. And a blank active file would limit context quality, but Copilot Chat can still respond to a direct chat prompt even without rich file context — that alone wouldn't typically produce zero suggestions across every request.

question: As the organization owner on a Copilot Business plan, your org wants to centrally disable MCP server support for every team member due to security/compliance concerns. How do you do this?
options: A) Go to Organization settings → Copilot → Policies, and set the 'MCP servers on GitHub' policy to disabled
B) Create a repo-level .vscode/mcp.json file with no servers defined and enforce it via a GitHub Actions script
C) Let each member individually disable MCP servers in their own personal Copilot settings
D) Upgrade to Copilot Enterprise, since Business doesn't support organization-wide policies at all
explanation: Business-tier organization owners can centrally manage feature policies — including the specific 'MCP servers on GitHub' policy under Organization settings → Copilot → Policies — and disabling it prevents MCP use across the org even if an individual member tries to turn it on themselves. A per-repo config file enforced via a script doesn't achieve org-wide, centralized control the way a real policy toggle does, and it wouldn't reliably override every individual's attempt to enable MCP elsewhere. Leaving it to individual members to disable MCP in their own settings is exactly the opposite of centralized enforcement — it relies on voluntary compliance rather than an admin-enforced policy. And Business absolutely does support organization-wide policy management, including this specific MCP policy — an Enterprise upgrade isn't required for this particular control.

question: According to GitHub's own research, what documented productivity benefit has been associated with using Copilot while coding?
options: A) Copilot fully replaces the need to consult any documentation
B) Developers always write objectively more concise code when using Copilot
C) Copilot automatically resolves merge conflicts without any developer input
D) Developers complete tasks up to 55% faster when using Copilot
explanation: GitHub's own research cites developers completing tasks up to 55% faster when using Copilot — a documented, specific productivity statistic reflecting reduced time spent on routine coding tasks and staying in flow. Claiming it fully replaces the need to consult documentation overstates its role — Copilot supplements development, but developers still need to verify against official docs, especially for anything niche or recently changed. Claiming code is 'always' more concise isn't a documented, universal outcome — conciseness varies by context and isn't the core measured productivity benefit. And Copilot has no capability to autonomously resolve merge conflicts — that's a distinct Git/version-control task entirely outside its code-suggestion role.

question: Besides the main Copilot Chat panel, which of these represents a distinct entry point for accessing Copilot Chat within your IDE?
options: A) Attaching an image file to a chat message
B) Specifying a chat participant with @
C) Using the quick chat dropdown for a fast question
D) Using slash commands within a prompt
explanation: GitHub documents several distinct UI surfaces for reaching Copilot Chat beyond the docked chat panel — the quick chat dropdown (a lightweight, transient entry point for a fast question) and inline/terminal chat are the additional access locations. Options A, B, and D are prompt-level features you use once you're already inside a chat interaction (attaching context, invoking a participant, or triggering a slash command) — they aren't separate ways of *opening* Copilot Chat, they're things you do within it. The exam distinguishes 'where you access chat from' (surfaces) versus 'what you do inside chat' (features), and this question tests the former.

question: In Copilot Edit Mode in VS Code, how can you revert the changes made to a single edited file?
options: A) Double-click the file in the 'files changed' list
B) Use the 'Keep' and 'Undo' controls on the editor overlay for that file
C) Drag the file out of the Explorer panel
D) Use only a global Ctrl+Z across the entire workspace
explanation: Copilot Edit Mode surfaces per-file 'Keep' and 'Undo' controls directly on the editor overlay, letting you accept or revert one file's changes without touching others. There's also an 'Undo Last Edit' control in the Chat view title bar for reverting the most recent edit set. Option A (double-clicking the changed-files list) just opens/navigates to the file — it doesn't revert anything. Option C (dragging a file out of Explorer) is not a supported or safe way to discard edits and risks corrupting the workspace. Option D (global Ctrl+Z) is too coarse — it undoes the last keystroke-level action across the whole editor, not a scoped set of Copilot-generated edits to one file, and can undo unrelated work.

question: When writing integration tests with Copilot that involve external systems, what is the recommended core technique?
options: A) Bypass all external calls entirely in the tests
B) Manually stand up temporary external service endpoints for every test
C) Use mock objects to simulate dependencies and assert the simulated interactions occurred as expected
D) Test only the database communication layer, ignoring other externals
explanation: GitHub's testing guidance highlights mock objects as the core mechanism for integration tests: they simulate external dependencies (APIs, services) predictably and cheaply, and assertions then verify the code interacted with those mocks as expected — this is how you test integration logic without flaky, slow, or costly real network calls. Option A defeats the purpose of an integration test, which specifically targets the boundary with external systems. Option B is impractical and not the documented approach — standing up real temporary services per test is exactly what mocking avoids. Option D arbitrarily narrows scope to only the database, ignoring other external dependencies (APIs, message queues, etc.) that integration tests are meant to cover.

question: When adding an MCP server using the 'stdio' connection type in VS Code, which field is required that is NOT applicable to 'http' or 'sse' connection types?
options: A) url
B) command
C) headers
D) args
explanation: A 'stdio' MCP server runs as a local process, so VS Code needs a `command` to actually launch that executable — there's no remote endpoint to connect to, unlike http/sse. Option A (`url`) is exactly backwards: `url` is required for http/sse (remote endpoint connections), not for stdio, which runs locally. Option C (`headers`) applies only to http/sse for auth/metadata on a network request — irrelevant to a local process launch. Option D (`args`) is optional, not required — you can launch a stdio server with just a command and no arguments, so it doesn't fit the 'required and stdio-exclusive' criteria the question asks about. (Note: `envFile` is also stdio-specific but optional, not strictly required.)

question: Which of the following accurately describes how custom coding guidelines are configured for GitHub Copilot?
options: A) Path patterns can be defined using fnmatch syntax, and each guideline includes a description of up to 600 characters
B) Guidelines require a maximum length limit on their name
C) Guidelines support a configurable priority level that determines application order
D) Guidelines must be manually enabled for Copilot code completion after creation
explanation: Custom coding guidelines scope themselves to specific files/directories via fnmatch-style path patterns (the same globbing style used elsewhere in GitHub's content-exclusion tooling) and carry a description field capped at 600 characters to explain their intent. Option B fabricates a name-length constraint that isn't part of the documented setup — names just need to be unique, not length-restricted. Option C is false — guidelines don't have a configurable priority/ordering system; they're applied based on scope and path pattern matching, not ranked priority. Option D is false — guidelines apply automatically once defined and scoped; there's no separate manual 'enable for code completion' toggle required after creation.

question: In VS Code, how do you initiate a GitHub Copilot code review of your local changes?
options: A) Only via the Command Palette, for both staged and unstaged changes
B) Via dedicated action buttons next to the 'Changes' (unstaged) and staged-changes lists in the Source Control panel
C) By navigating the Source Control interface to review an individual code block
D) Only staged changes can be reviewed, and only via the Command Palette
explanation: Copilot's IDE code-review capability is integrated directly into the Source Control panel: there's an action button next to the unstaged 'Changes' list and a separate one next to the staged-changes list, letting you trigger a review scoped to whichever set of modifications you choose. Options A and D wrongly route this through the Command Palette — that's not where the review is triggered from. Option C conflates two different actions: reviewing a specific code block is done inline in the editor (via a code action/lightbulb), not by 'navigating' Source Control, which is instead where you trigger reviews of staged/unstaged file sets. This tests precise recall of which UI surface maps to which review scope.

question: When an MCP server configured in VS Code fails, how do you access its detailed runtime logs for troubleshooting?
options: A) Via the Problems panel and the Debug Console
B) Via the Extensions view details and the Tool output window
C) Via the error notification in the Chat view and the 'MCP: List Servers' command, which exposes the server's output
D) Via the status bar icon and the Integrated Terminal
explanation: VS Code surfaces an MCP server failure as an error notification within the Chat view, and the 'MCP: List Servers' command lets you select the failing server and view its detailed output/log for diagnosis. Option A (Problems panel/Debug Console) targets language diagnostics and script debugging, not MCP server process logs. Option B (Extensions view/Tool output window) doesn't map to MCP's documented troubleshooting flow — MCP servers aren't managed like installed extensions. Option D (status bar icon/Integrated Terminal) isn't the documented MCP-specific mechanism; the terminal shows whatever process you manually ran, not the MCP server's internal log stream exposed through VS Code's own tooling.

question: For subscription-based network routing, which hostnames must be included in an organization's corporate firewall allowlist for Copilot access?
options: A) copilot.github.com and github.com only
B) *.business.githubcopilot.com and *.enterprise.githubcopilot.com
C) *.individual.githubcopilot.com only
D) github.com only, since all Copilot traffic routes through it
explanation: GitHub's subscription-based network routing uses plan-specific hostnames — *.business.githubcopilot.com for Business-licensed traffic and *.enterprise.githubcopilot.com for Enterprise-licensed traffic — so an org managing firewall access for Business/Enterprise seat holders needs both allowlisted. Option A's 'copilot.github.com' isn't the documented routing hostname pattern. Option C's *.individual.githubcopilot.com is the hostname for personal/individual-plan traffic, not organization-managed seats, so it's the wrong tier for a corporate firewall configuring org-licensed access. Option D understates the requirement — github.com alone doesn't cover the plan-specific Copilot model-request routing domains.

question: How are base-model chat interactions counted differently for Free-plan vs. paid-plan GitHub Copilot users?
options: A) Paid-plan users get unlimited base-model chat that doesn't draw from their premium-request allowance, while each Free-plan chat interaction counts as 1 premium request
B) Free users get 2,000 unlimited base-model chat requests monthly as part of their plan
C) Paid users' base-model code completions count against their monthly premium allowance
D) All interactions, regardless of plan or model, consistently consume premium requests
explanation: Paid Copilot plans include unlimited base-model chat and code completions that don't draw down the premium-request allowance — only premium (advanced) model usage consumes that quota. Free-plan users, by contrast, don't get an 'unlimited base model' carve-out for chat; each base-model chat interaction on Free counts as 1 premium request against their small monthly allotment. Option B misapplies the 2,000-completions figure (which covers code completions, not chat) as if it were an unlimited chat allowance. Option C reverses the paid-plan rule — base-model completions on paid plans are unlimited and premium-allowance-free, not counted against it. Option D is too absolute — it ignores the documented base-model/premium-model distinction entirely.

question: After VS Code's chat agent mode proposes code changes, how can you review or manage them?
options: A) Accept or discard edits per file, or use the 'Undo' control in the Chat view title bar to revert the most recent edit set
B) All pending edits are automatically discarded if VS Code is closed
C) Reverting edits from a specific request requires changing a VS Code setting first
D) Edits are accepted instantly the moment they stream into the editor
explanation: Agent mode gives you per-file accept/discard control over proposed edits, plus a dedicated 'Undo' control in the Chat view title bar to revert the most recently applied edit set — mirroring the same review controls documented for Edit Mode. Option B is a fabricated behavior; closing VS Code doesn't automatically discard pending edits as a documented feature. Option C is false — reverting doesn't require a settings change; it's a direct UI action via the accept/discard controls or the title-bar Undo. Option D is incorrect — edits stream in as proposals for review, not as instantly finalized changes; that's precisely why accept/discard controls exist.

question: When reviewing GitHub Copilot usage within your enterprise account, what information is available?
options: A) The total number of Copilot seats currently assigned across all organizations, and an org-level breakdown of seats carried over from prior billing cycles
B) Real-time code completion statistics for individual users
C) Daily cost estimates broken down per individual Copilot user
D) The specific internal calculation method used for monthly billed seat usage
explanation: Enterprise-level Copilot license usage reporting shows aggregate seat counts across all member organizations and an organization-level breakdown, including seats carried over from prior billing cycles — this is the documented scope of the enterprise license-usage view. Option B overstates granularity — the view doesn't expose real-time, per-user code-completion telemetry; that level of detail isn't part of the license/seat usage reporting surface. Option C (daily per-user cost estimates) isn't a documented feature of this view — billing is aggregated, not itemized per user per day. Option D is a distractor — the exact internal billing calculation methodology isn't exposed to admins; they see results (counts, seats), not the underlying computation.

question: Which two GitHub Copilot plans include exactly 300 premium requests per month?
options: A) Copilot Business and Copilot Pro
B) Copilot Free and Copilot Pro+
C) Copilot Pro+ and Copilot Enterprise
D) Copilot Free and Copilot Enterprise
explanation: Copilot Pro and Copilot Business both include a 300 premium-requests-per-month allowance per user — the same figure despite one being an individual plan and the other an org-managed plan. Copilot Free sits much lower (a small monthly allotment, not 300), Copilot Pro+ sits much higher (1,500/month, reflecting its premium-model-heavy positioning), and Copilot Enterprise has its own distinct allowance tier. This is exactly the kind of specific numeric figure GH-300 likes to test directly — knowing which tiers share the same allowance number, rather than assuming allowance scales strictly with plan cost.

question: As an organization owner, which sequence of actions is a valid way to obtain GitHub Copilot activity insights?
options: A) Use the REST API to list all assigned users, then query each user's individual telemetry data for usage frequency
B) Navigate to organization settings, select the Copilot Access page, view the overview, then download a CSV report for details
C) Use the GraphQL API to query user usage metrics and estimated cost directly from the organization dashboard
D) Access the organization's insights dashboard, select a Copilot tab, and filter activity logs by last code suggestion date
explanation: The documented path for an org owner reviewing Copilot activity is through organization Settings → the Copilot Access page, which provides an overview and a CSV export option for detailed per-user activity data — a UI-driven workflow, not an ad-hoc API composition. Option A misdescribes the REST API's role — there's no documented per-user telemetry query endpoint you assemble this way; seat/activity data comes from dedicated seat-listing endpoints, not raw telemetry queries. Option C invents a GraphQL usage/cost query that isn't part of Copilot's documented API surface. Option D references a generic 'organization insights dashboard' with a Copilot tab that isn't the actual documented UI location — Copilot activity review lives specifically under Copilot Access settings.

question: How can you initiate Copilot Edit Mode in VS Code?
options: A) Select 'Edit' from the mode selector in the Chat view panel, or use the vscode://GitHub.Copilot-Chat/chat?mode=edit URL scheme
B) Use the 'Revert Last Edit' control in the editor overlay
C) Run the 'Accept All Edits' command palette action
D) Add the '#codebase' keyword without first entering Edit Mode
explanation: Edit Mode is entered either through the mode selector in the Chat view panel (the standard in-UI path) or via a dedicated VS Code URL scheme (vscode://GitHub.Copilot-Chat/chat?mode=edit) that can be triggered externally, e.g. from documentation links or automation. Option B ('Revert Last Edit') is a control you use *after* you're already in an active edit session to undo changes — it doesn't initiate the session. Option C ('Accept All Edits') is likewise a post-generation action for finalizing proposed changes, not a way to start Edit Mode. Option D describes using a context keyword outside Edit Mode entirely, which doesn't launch the mode — it's just a chat-context reference usable in Ask mode too.

question: Which of the following is a valid, documented way to configure custom code-generation instructions in GitHub Copilot?
options: A) Store instructions in a .github/copilot-instructions.md file, or use the github.copilot.chat.codeGeneration.instructions setting in settings.json
B) Include custom instructions directly in the settings.sync file for team sharing
C) Define instructions using inline comments in the source code files
D) Only one of these two mechanisms is officially supported; the other has been deprecated
explanation: VS Code's documentation confirms two valid, coexisting mechanisms for code-generation instructions: the repository-level .github/copilot-instructions.md file, and the github.copilot.chat.codeGeneration.instructions setting configured in settings.json — giving developers flexibility depending on whether they want repo-wide or workspace/user-level configuration. Option B fabricates a settings.sync-based sharing mechanism that isn't documented. Option C is wrong — inline source comments aren't the mechanism for *persistent, reusable* custom instructions; that's what the dedicated instructions file/setting is for. Option D is false — both mechanisms are current and supported simultaneously, not a deprecated/replacement pair.

question: What is the purpose of the `gh auth login` command in relation to Copilot in the CLI?
options: A) To download the latest version of the Copilot CLI extension
B) To enable data collection for Copilot CLI analytics
C) To grant Copilot CLI permission to access all your private repositories
D) To authenticate with GitHub so Copilot in the CLI can function correctly
explanation: `gh auth login` establishes GitHub authentication for the `gh` CLI, which Copilot's CLI integration depends on to identify the user and their entitlements before it can function. Option A confuses authentication with installation — a separate step (installing the extension/binary) precedes login. Option B fabricates an analytics-opt-in purpose that isn't what this command does. Option C overstates its effect — authenticating doesn't itself broadly grant Copilot standing access to 'all' private repos; repository access is governed by the user's own existing GitHub permissions, and Copilot only processes what's relevant to the active session/context, not a blanket repo-access grant.

question: For a web app needing Spanish, German, and French support, how can Copilot best assist with translation/internationalization (i18n) while maintaining quality?
options: A) Use Copilot to translate only UI elements, keeping business logic and dynamic content in the original language
B) Use Copilot to help create language resource files (.json/.po) for different locales while manually verifying translations for accuracy
C) Use Copilot to automatically translate strings by typing English text and selecting its suggestion
D) Rely entirely on Copilot to generate translation files for all supported languages without further validation
explanation: Copilot is genuinely useful for generating the structural boilerplate of resource files and initial translation drafts, but manual verification by a native speaker or professional translator remains essential since Copilot lacks true linguistic/cultural understanding needed for user-facing text accuracy. Option A conflates a design decision (what to translate) with how Copilot assists, and doesn't reflect Copilot's actual capability scope. Option C describes only a narrow slice of the workflow (single-string suggestions) and omits the critical verification step, oversimplifying the full i18n process. Option D is risky and irresponsible — fully trusting AI-generated translations without any human review could produce inaccurate, awkward, or even offensive text in a global-facing application.

question: After installing GitHub Copilot CLI, which command verifies it is correctly installed and available in your terminal?
options: A) gh copilot test
B) gh copilot status
C) copilot --check
D) gh extension list
explanation: Copilot CLI is implemented as a `gh` CLI extension, so `gh extension list` — the standard command for listing all installed gh extensions — will show it if installed correctly, confirming successful setup. Option A ('gh copilot test') isn't a documented command for installation verification. Option B ('gh copilot status') is a plausible-sounding but non-standard command for this purpose — Copilot subcommands are for *using* Copilot (explain/suggest), not for checking whether the extension itself is present. Option C is wrong because Copilot CLI is invoked through `gh`, not as a standalone `copilot` executable — there's no `copilot --check` command.

question: A financial services company has a fully air-gapped development environment with no external internet access. What should they recognize about using GitHub Copilot for Business?
options: A) Copilot can be configured for offline use through a GitHub Enterprise Server
B) Copilot can generate suggestions locally but only after an initial model download and registration
C) Copilot for Business requires an active internet connection and will not function in an air-gapped environment
D) Copilot supports air-gapped environments as long as the developer's IDE is configured beforehand
explanation: Copilot for Business depends on a live connection between the IDE and GitHub's cloud-hosted Copilot proxy service; since air-gapped environments block outbound internet access, Copilot simply cannot function there — a hard architectural constraint, not a configuration option. Option A is false — there's no offline-capable configuration via GitHub Enterprise Server that lets Copilot's cloud-hosted inference work without connectivity. Option B is false — there's no one-time model download that enables ongoing local generation; the model remains cloud-hosted and requires per-request connectivity. Option D is false — no IDE-side configuration can substitute for the required live connection to GitHub's cloud infrastructure.

question: A developer notices several Copilot-generated unit tests fail immediately, even before running the full test suite. What situation most likely caused this?
options: A) They used Copilot immediately after changing their code editor theme
B) They asked Copilot to create tests in a file that contained only comments and no executable code
C) They ran Copilot in a branch that had no open pull requests
D) They used Copilot to write tests before the target functions were fully implemented or documented
explanation: Copilot generates tests using context from your codebase; if the target functions are incomplete, missing parameter details, or lack documentation, Copilot may fill gaps with incorrect assumptions about behavior, producing broken or irrelevant tests — a direct, realistic cause of immediate test failures. Option A (editor theme) is a cosmetic setting with no bearing on Copilot's code-generation logic or test quality. Option C (branch's PR status) is unrelated — whether a branch has open pull requests doesn't affect Copilot's ability to generate valid tests from the code it can see. Option B is a plausible but less likely scenario in this context — a file with only comments and no executable code would more likely yield no test suggestions at all rather than specifically 'several tests that fail right away,' which points more directly to incomplete/undocumented target functions as the cause.
